title: AVERAGEIFS Multiple Criteria
description: AVERAGEIFS multiple criteria lets you average cells that satisfy two or more conditions at once. Learn the syntax, real examples, and how it differs from AVERAGEIF and SUMIFS.
intro: AVERAGEIFS averages values only when every one of its criteria is true, which makes it perfect for questions like 'what is the average sales amount for Product A in the West region?' This guide covers the syntax, walks through worked examples with several conditions, and shows where AVERAGEIFS beats both AVERAGEIF and SUMIFS.
prerequisites: Familiarity with cell ranges and basic criteria
The difference between a value range and a criteria range

sections.title: AVERAGEIFS Syntax — Every Range Must Be the Same Size
sections.content: AVERAGEIFS takes the average range first, then pairs of criteria range and criteria. All ranges must have the same dimensions, or Excel returns #VALUE!. A row is included in the average only if it satisfies every condition you list. The function is AND-based: more criteria means a narrower (usually smaller) average.

steps.name: Pick the average range
steps.text: This is the column of numbers you want to average.

steps.name: Add each criteria range + condition pair
steps.text: List them in any order after the average range; every range must match the size of the average range.

tips: Think of AVERAGEIFS as SUMIFS divided by COUNTIFS for the same conditions.

sections.title: Example: Average by Product AND Region
sections.content: Suppose column A holds Product, column C holds Region, and column D holds the Amount sold. To average only the amounts where Product is A and Region is West, you give AVERAGEIFS both conditions. Only rows meeting both are averaged.

example.result: Returns the average of column D where Product = 'A' AND Region = 'West'
example.explanation: Each criteria pair is AND-ed. If no row matches both, the formula returns #DIV/0! instead of an average.

tips: Reference cells instead of hard-coding text, e.g. A2:A100, G1, so you can change the criteria without editing the formula.

sections.title: Numeric and Operator Criteria
sections.content: Criteria are not limited to exact matches. You can use operators such as >, >=, <, and <> by joining them to a value, and you can mix a numeric condition with a text condition in the same formula. Wildcards (* and ?) work for partial text matches.

example.result: Average of column D where Amount > 100 AND Region = 'West'
example.explanation: The ">100" criteria is a text string; Excel evaluates it as a greater-than comparison. Use "Pro*" to average only products whose names start with 'Pro'.

tips: When the threshold lives in a cell, concatenate: ">"&G2 so the cutoff updates automatically.

sections.title: AVERAGEIFS vs AVERAGEIF vs SUMIFS
sections.content: AVERAGEIF handles a single condition and puts the average range LAST, while AVERAGEIFS takes the average range FIRST and supports many conditions. SUMIFS mirrors AVERAGEIFS exactly in argument order but returns a sum instead of an average. If you already know SUMIFS, AVERAGEIFS will feel identical except for the first range.

example.result: Sum of column D (not the average) for the same two conditions
example.explanation: Same conditions as the AVERAGEIFS example, but a total. Divide this SUMIFS by a COUNTIFS with the same criteria to reproduce AVERAGEIFS manually.

tips: Prefer AVERAGEIFS over a SUMIFS/COUNTIFS pair — it is one function and avoids divide-by-zero handling.

sections.title: Handling the #DIV/0! When Nothing Matches
sections.content: When no row satisfies all criteria, AVERAGEIFS returns #DIV/0! because it has nothing to divide by. Wrap the formula in IFERROR to show a clean zero or message instead of an error, which keeps dashboards tidy.

example.result: 0 when no row matches both criteria, otherwise the average
example.explanation: IFERROR catches the #DIV/0! and substitutes 0 (or any value you choose) so reports stay readable.

tips: Use a text fallback like "No data" instead of 0 if a blank average would be misleading.

summary: AVERAGEIFS is the conditional-average workhorse: give it an average range plus any number of criteria-range pairs, and it averages only the rows that satisfy all conditions. Remember the average range comes first, all ranges must be the same size, and a no-match result is a #DIV/0! you can tame with IFERROR.
